Threat.value: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Memory.value: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning

Negative Appraisals.value: The people responsible have faced no consequences
I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable.
I can't stop bad things from happening to me

issues.item: Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'I can talk about what happened very easily' sits in tension with 'Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time' in a severe childhood domestic-violence PTSD profile. Marked ease of verbal access is hard to reconcile with intensely distressing recall as a defining memory style, especially when the formulation emphasizes reciprocal Threat–Memory and Threat–Negative Appraisals links rather than a well-processed narrative memory. The pair could occasionally coexist, but here the contradiction is strong enough to question coherence of the selected memory items.

issues.item: Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, these two items describe opposing states during recall—detached/numb recall versus recall that consistently re-evokes the same terror. Both can occur across different moments in PTSD, but presented together as co-selected core memory descriptors without qualification they are internally tensioned and are the clearest coherence problem in the profile. The rest of the profile is broadly plausible for severe PTSD after witnessing childhood domestic violence, and the Threat/Negative Appraisals linkage fits the formulation.

issues.item: Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
issues.explanation: The threat items imply a current expectation of direct interpersonal harm from others and a generalized startle/hypervigilance profile, whereas the trauma is witnessing domestic violence in childhood. That can be possible, but in this profile the danger focus is on strangers/other people harming the patient, which is not well anchored by the other nodes.

issues.item: Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
issues.explanation: The negative appraisal items focus on justice/accountability for perpetrators, but for childhood witnessed domestic violence this emphasis is somewhat hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile, which otherwise centers on reliving terror and generalized threat. These appraisals do not connect well to the selected threat items or to the formulation's strong Threat↔Negative Appraisals linkage.

issues.item: Threat: Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
issues.explanation: For childhood witnessed domestic violence, hypervigilance and bodily alarm are plausible, but specifically watching other people for signs that they might harm me implies a generalized interpersonal threat focused on the self. That is harder to reconcile with the rest of the profile, which centers on recall terror and injustice about what was witnessed rather than a coherent belief that others are currently likely to attack him.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: No Accountability: The people responsible have faced no consequences
issues.explanation: The appraisal that the responsible people faced no consequences is plausible in this trauma type, but paired with 'nothing has been done about it' it suggests an ongoing justice-focused grievance. This sits awkwardly with the threat and memory items, which emphasize re-experiencing terror rather than a clinically coherent meaning pattern linking current threat to the childhood domestic violence exposure.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Injustice: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it
issues.explanation: 'What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it' is somewhat mismatched to witnessed domestic violence in childhood because the trauma type is witnessing violence between others rather than a direct assault on the patient. While survivors can absolutely personalize the injustice, the phrasing 'happened to me' combined with the justice-focused theme is less coherent with the rest of the selected items than appraisals about safety, powerlessness, or lasting damage would be.

vignette:
Arjun was eight years old the first time he saw his father strike his mother. He remembered the sound-the flat crack of an open palm against her cheek-and the silence that followed, heavier than the blow. He had frozen in the doorway, his small body unwilling to move, his voice locked in his throat. No one came. No one ever came. His father faced no consequences; neighbors pretended not to hear, and his mother never spoke of it. Arjun grew up believing that the world was a place where bad things happened without anyone stepping in, and that he was powerless to stop them.

Now thirty-six and an accountant for a mid-sized firm in Chicago, Arjun lives alone in a one-bedroom apartment, five years divorced. He spends most of his days in a cubicle, hunched over spreadsheets, grateful for the quiet. But the quiet is never safe. Without warning, a coworker's raised voice across the hall-someone laughing too loudly-can hurl him back into that doorway. The memory returns not as a story he can tell, but as a visceral crash: the smell of his mother's perfume, the sting of his own held breath, the terror pouring through him like ice water. He cannot put it into words. He only feels it, and his body does what it learned to do: his heart pounds, his palms sweat, his muscles coil as if an attack is coming.

That feeling of constant threat has become the wallpaper of his life. Arjun's body stays tense, ready to react to danger that rarely arrives. He scans every room for exits, every conversation for a shift in tone. He has come to believe that if he lets his guard down, something terrible will happen again. This hypervigilance, in turn, keeps the memories raw. Every sudden noise, every raised eyebrow, every moment of unexpected silence triggers without warning the same old terror, and he is eight years old again, watching helplessly.

The cycle tightens around him. Because the people who hurt his family never faced consequences, Arjun is certain that nothing he does matters. He used to be a happy child, but now he is always miserable, convinced that bad things will happen no matter how carefully he lives. When a memory crashes in-unbidden, wordless-it confirms his helplessness. And when he feels his body tense and his mind race, he tells himself that he is right to be afraid, because the world is unforgiving. The conviction that the world was unforgiving kept pulling him back into the memory of that silence after the slap, as if the past itself had to prove him right.

These beliefs have shaped his daily life. He avoids social gatherings, declines team projects, and leaves the office the moment his shift ends. His marriage ended because his wife could no longer reach him; he spent evenings locked in himself, certain that opening up would only invite more pain. At work, he is known as competent but distant. He once panicked during a budget meeting when two colleagues argued over numbers; he fled to the restroom and stood shaking over the sink, unable to speak. That was the moment he began to wonder if something was seriously wrong.

What finally brought Arjun to therapy was a string of such incidents-one too many mornings waking with his fists clenched, one too many nights lying awake listening for sounds that were not there. He is exhausted. He is afraid that he will never feel safe, never trust his own body again. But what frightens him most is the idea that he will pass this on, that his own children-if he ever lets himself have them-will grow up in the same invisible fog. He came because he wants to stop the cycle, even if he is not sure how.

violations.explanation: The vignette does not show that negative appraisals (e.g., beliefs of powerlessness or that the world is unforgiving) directly cause or trigger the trauma memory. Instead, the memory arrives unbidden from external cues and then confirms the appraisals, but the reverse causal direction is absent.

vignette_attempts.feedback:

- Negative Appraisals → Memory: The vignette does not show that negative appraisals (e.g., beliefs of powerlessness or that the world is unforgiving) directly cause or trigger the trauma memory. Instead, the memory arrives unbidden from external cues and then confirms the appraisals, but the reverse causal direction is absent.
  e.g. "The belief that she was permanently changed kept bringing her back to the moment it had happened, as if she needed to locate exactly where she had been lost."
  e.g. "Telling herself that she should have seen it coming made the memory more vivid and easier to find — it sat there waiting, proof of her failure."
  e.g. "The conviction that she was weak fed directly into the flashback, colouring it, making it worse: she wasn't just there again, she was there again and helpless."
